newsitem.title: MOZAMBIQUE: Mozambican gas project lacks buyers, under threat.
newsitem.headline: Mozambican gas project lacks buyers, under threat.

text.p: Plans to exploit large reserves of natural gas in southern Mozambique are under threat because no firm buyer can be found, a senior South African government source told Reuters on Monday.
The Mozambican government has a production sharing agreement for the Pande gas field with American energy giant Enron, under which Enron must find buyers.

The agreement was reached in 1995, and there have already been two extensions to give Enron time to come up with a scheme that would make it possible to exploit the field, 700 km (450 miles) north of Maputo city, at a profit.
The second of these extensions expired last Thursday.
The source, who works in the energy sector, backed statements attributed to Mozambique's Minister of Mineral Resources and Energy, John Kachamila, in Monday's issue of the Maputo daily Metical.
Kachamila reportedly said the government was open to a third extension of six or eight months, "but no conclusion has yet been reached".
Neither Kachamila nor local Enron officials were available for comment.
The only feasible clients for the gas are in South Africa but Enron has not yet been able to break into that market.
With no definitive South African buyer the huge investments required to extract and transport the gas would not be justified, Reuters' source said.

Pande gas could be used at a proposed Maputo-based iron ore reduction plant. Iron ore slurry would be piped 300 km (200 miles) from the Phalaborwa mine in South Africa to produce four million tonnes of iron a year.

But Kachamila has said the project could use only a small amount of Pande's two trillon cubic feet of gas, and has problems because Phalaborwa ore contain impurities, copper and phosphate, which reduce its value.

The source, speaking in Maputo, said that if the Phalaborwa project fails, Enron has little option but to try to sell the gas to the South African state energy company Sasol, whose current activities includes gas production and sales.
Kachamila said that Sasol would not switch to Mozambican gas unless it had a share in the production agreement and in the gas pipeline that would be built from Pande to South Africa.
Sasol would not accept dependence on an energy source over which it had no control, Kachamila said.
